KOTA BARU: Coastal erosion caused by strong waves during the Northeast Monsoon has exposed an old rubbish dump at Pantai Dasar, Sabak, here, more than 10 years after it was buried.
The erosion has left various types of waste scattered along the shoreline, raising concerns over environmental pollution.
The recent appearance of siput kemudi or kerang kapak at Pantai Sabak and Pantai Dasar has also drawn public attention to the existence of the old dumpsite.
It is believed to have ceased operations more than 10 years ago after the land was purchased by a private party and covered with soil.
However, coastal erosion over the past few years has washed away the soil, exposing the buried waste.
Checks also found that a British-built defence bunker, constructed ahead of World War 2 near the site, had been affected by erosion.
Resident Che Mohd Hakim Che Hasim, 25, said the dumpsite had long been abandoned, although its existence had been known to villagers for years.
"However, it was only after the kerang kapak appeared and the issue went viral that the public became aware of the old dumpsite right beside the beach," he said at Kampung Pantai Dasar yesterday.
He added that the secluded site was on a privately owned land.
Trader Nazura Jusoh, 40, said the old dumpsite needed immediate attention and proper management to prevent more rubbish from entering the sea.
Retired civil servant Nik Zainal Abidin Che Harun, 66, said the beach near the old dumpsite was scenic and could become a tourist attraction.
b609156aea2af472: CARDIFF: Portugal shrugged off a spirited Wales and the distraction of Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement with a 3-2 win in Cardiff to secure top spot in Nations League Group A4.

KUALA LUMPUR: Two years ago, Datuk Dr M. Periasamy's grandson asked if he could really finish a doctorate at his age.

Yesterday, the 77-year-old political analyst proved that age was no barrier, receiving his doctorate in political science from Universiti Malaya (UM) after completing the programme in five semesters and earning a Graduate on Time award.
Periasamy said he was overjoyed, having once doubted whether he would complete his higher education in his lifetime.
"I am very happy because I thought I might not be able to finish it as I am already 77.
"At first, my grandson asked me, 'Grandpa, you are getting old, so can you complete this study?'
"But I felt that with the experience I had gained over the years, I could manage the analysis required for my thesis," he said after UM's 66th convocation.
Present was UM chancellor Sultan of Perak Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah.
The convocation, involving 11,852 graduates, runs over 17 sessions until Nov 26.
Periasamy, a former civil servant, said he initially felt like giving up but gradually gained confidence after a few months, realising that his experience could help him complete the research.
He said he pursued the doctorate to gain greater confidence in writing political articles and analysis, adding that the title of "Dr" would lend further credibility to his work.
Meanwhile, two other graduates completed a joint PhD programme between UM and the University of New South Wales, Sydney.
Dr Nurul Jannah Zamberi, from Kluang, Johor, who graduated in biomedical engineering, said it took her about five years to complete her doctorate.
She said she had completed her undergraduate studies in the United States before returning to Malaysia, where she came across the joint PhD opportunity offered by UM.
"I wanted to further my studies, and then UM offered this joint PhD programme. I decided to apply and was fortunate to be accepted."
The mother of one said she had since joined UM as a lecturer after submitting her thesis about a year ago.
Another graduate, Dr Ooi Jia Hui, from Ipoh, completed the same joint PhD programme in 3½ years and is now a post-doctoral researcher at the University of Sydney.
She said losing her grandparents while pursuing her doctorate had been one of the most difficult periods of her studies.
"It was very hard for me but I am glad I made it through.
"I had promised them that I would complete my PhD, and that promise kept me going."

e76baf1a121aac1f: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday.

ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword.

Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.

KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's online job offerings have risen 17.8 per cent to 654,655 in the third quarter, with the highest demand for advertising and marketing professionals.
The Statistics Department said 95,102 companies had advertised job vacancies during the quarter, up from 79,510 in the second quarter.
Professional posts accounted for the largest offerings, at 47.1 per cent or 308,137 vacancies, compared with 285,907 in the preceding quarter.
Technicians and associate professionals recorded 110,180 job offerings, followed by managers with 96,442.
Among individual occupations, advertising and marketing professionals topped the list with 44,989 offerings.
This was followed by administrative associate professionals (29,708), managing directors and chief executives (27,915), accountants and auditors (23,562), and software developers (18,109).
The services sector continued to account for the largest share of online job offerings, advertising 325,520 vacancies or 49.7 per cent of the total, compared with 43.9 per cent in the second quarter.
Wholesale and retail trade and motor vehicle repair recorded the highest number of job offerings at 90,613 vacancies.
This was followed by professional, scientific and technical activities (50,220), other service activities (37,518), administrative and support service activities (35,263), and manufacturing (30,495).
In the technical and vocational education and training field, technicians recorded the highest number of offerings at 8,306.
This was followed by sales managers (5,001) and marketing executives (4,810).
Technicians also topped demand in the science, technology, engineering and mathematics field, with 8,306 job offerings, followed by engineers (4,343) and quantity surveyors (4,294).
Under the critical occupations List, sales executives recorded the highest demand with 9,772 job offerings, followed by assistant managers (9,520) and account executives (9,290).

The Statistics Department revealed these figures in its report entitled "Big Data Analytics: Job Market Insights Online Job Offerings Advertised in Malaysia (Q3 2026)", which it says provides jobseekers with insights into demand across occupations and economic sectors.

e6e38fa0ebf8cc1d: LONDON: Hundreds of people protested on Tuesday outside a talk by controversial academic Nathan Cofnas, a self-described "race-realist" accused of racism, held at a University of Oxford college.

The US academic was suspended — and later reinstated — as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Ghent in Belgium in August after making plagiarism accusations against black Cambridge professor Jason Arday earlier this year.
Arday was later found dead at his home after resigning from his post amid the escalating scandal.

A petition opposing his Tuesday evening event at Oriel College, organised by the Oxford Reform student society — linked to the national hard-right Reform UK party — attracted tens of thousands of signatures.

Meanwhile, the Stand Up To Racism activist group organised a demonstration that drew hundreds of people, some wearing face masks and many carrying placards bearing slogans such as "Nathan Cofnas not welcome" and "Remember Professor Jason Arday".
UK media reported that some protesters appeared to try to block the entrance gates to prevent attendees from entering the college ahead of the talk.
Afterwards, some purported attendees posted on social media that they were unable to leave because demonstrators were blocking the exits.
Footage of the protests shared online showed police in attendance as crowds gathered outside.
"Nathan Cofnas is blockaded in Oxford by thousands of anti-fascists," Stand Up To Racism posted on X, alongside a video of the scene.
Cofnas has courted controversy for years over his eugenics-linked views tying race to intelligence.
In 2024, his research affiliation with Cambridge ended amid accusations of racism.
Tuesday's event was entitled "Is DEI Undermining Higher Education?", referring to Diversity, Equality and Inclusion policies.
Ahead of the event, Oxford Reform had defended it, saying it was "committed to broadening participation in university life" by inviting such speakers.
Oriel College said in a statement that hosting the event on its grounds "does not imply endorsement by the College of the views of its speakers".

An online petition calling on the university or college to "cancel Nathan Cofnas's invitation to speak" and urging the institutions to protect "Black students and staff" had received nearly 33,000 signatures by late Tuesday.
"Ideas platformed at Oxford do not stay in the lecture theatre. They travel through social media and political debate, carrying the University's authority," the petition stated.
d13e4936fd974660: JERUSALEM: Israel's parliament voted on Tuesday to elect a new speaker opposed to Benjamin Netanyahu's agenda, a potential first step towards rolling back the prime minister's divisive political agenda even as his main rival struggles to form a government.

Parties led by Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor in an inconclusive October election, voted to install Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot's centre-right Yashar party. Kahana received 66 votes, while 52 lawmakers voted for another candidate, according to the parliament spokesperson's office.
Kahana replaces Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party.
"The Knesset of Israel is the home of all citizens of the State of Israel, and I intend to be the Speaker for everyone," Kahana said in his inaugural speech.
In Israel's unicameral 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, the speakership is a powerful position that wields considerable influence, including over which legislation is brought to a vote.
Kahana will be able to advance bills prioritised by the Eisenkot-led bloc and other parties backing the former general in his bid to become prime minister.

These include establishing an independent inquiry into the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas attack, which Netanyahu has opposed; imposing term limits on the prime minister; and repealing laws passed by the previous Netanyahu-led government that critics said curtailed the powers of the judiciary.

Netanyahu's Likud party condemned the vote, saying lawmakers had elected Kahana with "the votes of terror supporters". Throughout the election campaign, Netanyahu attacked Israel's Arab-led parties, saying they represented an existential threat to Israel, in remarks the parties condemned as racist and discriminatory.
Members of the Eisenkot-led bloc have also been appointed to chair several key parliamentary committees, which play an important role in advancing legislation.

The parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government, after a deadlocked general election on October 27 stripped Netanyahu of his majority but left his main rivals with no clear path to power.

President Isaac Herzog has tasked Eisenkot, who heads the centre-right Yashar political party, with forming a government. However, the former military chief also lacks a majority and will likely have to compromise on some campaign promises to secure the support needed to form a government.

Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a government is formed. His right-wing Likud alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties performed better than expected in the election but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats.

Eisenkot's Yashar party and its patchwork coalition partners hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in parties representing Israel's Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Eisenkot in their strong opposition to Netanyahu.
If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.

Netanyahu has sought to cast doubt on the election results by baselessly alleging voter fraud by Arabs, who make up a fifth of the population. Election officials have said they are investigating potential misconduct but have seen no evidence of fraud that could have influenced the outcome.

Israel's Channel 12 News reported on Sunday that law enforcement authorities were investigating whether officials in Netanyahu's office had deliberately planted information that prompted an inquiry into alleged vote-buying in Arab communities.
Netanyahu's office dismissed the Channel 12 report as "false".
5fe8112e7b116a7f: NEW YORK: US stocks extended their tech-driven slide on Tuesday as investors braced for Nvidia's earnings, expected just after the bell.

Those jitters intensified ahead of Anthropic's mammoth IPO, expected on Wednesday, which is targeted to raise as much as US$1.4 trillion.
All three major US stock indexes closed sharply lower.
The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq notched their first four-day streak of declines since September.

"Every sector in the S&P is down," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice-president at Wealthspire Advisors, in New York. "So clearly, it is a reflection of overall investor nervousness as opposed to being driven by a specific set of stocks, whether they're AI-related or not".
"It's a confluence of all of the events that are there, and it seems to be speculation-driven as opposed to fact-driven," Pursche added. "It's not all about Nvidia," he added.

The AI trade was already contending with popular opposition to large data centres when tech shares were rocked by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's ouster following revelations of his relationship with an alleged spy.
Investors are also impatient to see returns on hyperscalers' massive expenditures.
The Trump administration's plans to block imports of Chinese data centre equipment gained momentum in the wake of Huang's departure, despite opposition from Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and others.

Expectations leading up to Nvidia's results were sky-high. The company was projected to post 90.4% year-on-year earnings growth on revenue of US$109.11 billion. The stock ended the session in negative territory.

Enthusiasm over artificial intelligence helped send the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index's year-to-date gain as high as 106% in June, but that fervor has since lost steam. The index's gains so far this year have shrunk to about 34%.

Economic data released early in the session showed strong underlying retail sales, weakening industrial output and rising import prices, largely driven by spiking petroleum costs. Homebuilder sentiment plunged to its lowest level since April 2012.

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 75.96 points, or 1.02%, to end at 7,341.23 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 180.42 points, or 0.74%, to 24,329.34. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 859.71 points, or 1.67%, to 50,748.46.
On the sector level, software & services, airlines and banks were clear underperformers.
Intel fell after Nvidia cut its stake in the company by 25%.
Software shares were broadly lower, with Salesforce, Workday, Intuit and Adobe all losing ground.
Microsoft also declined on the day.
JPMorgan shares dipped after the company said insider Bregje de Best would succeed Jeremy Barnum as chief financial officer in early 2027.
Fed hints at aggressive rate hikes
Fed officials are increasingly suggesting that stubborn inflation has made the central bank more open to an aggressive US rate-hike path.
Markets are pricing in a near-certain 95.4% likelihood of a 25-basis-point increase in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
On Wednesday, minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's October meeting could help illuminate the central bank's approach to near-term monetary policy.

AFTER a four-year hiatus from Malaysian music award ceremonies, acclaimed singer-songwriter Yuna is open to returning to prestigious stages such as Anugerah Juara Lagu (AJL) and Anugerah Industri Muzik (AIM).
Having recently reached her 40th milestone, the songstress believes her latest studio album 'Senjata' deserves to compete since it was entirely produced in Malaysia.
Speaking at the album's launch, she expressed excitement about the creative freedom competitive platforms offer.

"This is a made-in-Malaysia album, so I feel it's only right that we compete in AJL and AIM. The most fun part about AJL is being given a stage and the creative freedom to present the song. So I told my team, if we enter AJL, I want a pirate ship on stage."
Being an independent artiste means she must carefully weigh time, budgets and team support before committing to large-scale competitions.

"If there is support and the opportunity arises, why not? Because I didn't make this music alone. I created it with my team, and they want to see me enter AJL. I am fine with it too, and it would be a fun experience. I'm doing it for the fans as well because I am indebted to them."
When asked which track she would put forward, Yuna hoped the titular song 'Senjata' would take centre stage as it held the closest place in her heart.

45a58f11968d9021: WASHINGTON: Former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang said Tuesday he wanted his job back despite resigning over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, marking a new twist for the turmoil-hit AI chip giant hours before it releases a key earnings report.

Investors will scrutinise the results for indications that the artificial intelligence (AI) boom can withstand the Nvidia crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.
Huang, a leading promoter of AI, stepped down last week following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The upheaval has battered shares of Nvidia - until recently the world's most valuable publicly traded company - which is at the centre of an AI boom that has helped propel markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the globe.
Nvidia has lost US$700 billion in market value since the scandal broke, and Huang is to be questioned by US lawmakers on Dec 1 over national security concerns.

However, his fall triggered immediate calls from Elon Musk and other entrepreneurs for his return, and even president Donald Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Huang back at Nvidia, downplaying the spy allegations.

"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in his first statement since his resignation.

"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," he said.
Trump-Xi talks

The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, which starts this week in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Under Washington's new rules, data centers anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

The rules also require licenses to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil - countries the US commerce department says present a "higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips.

The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.
While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang's affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.

His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed - a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.
Business as usual ?
Tuesday's third quarter results, which are scheduled for 5pm Eastern time, will be the first presented under Nvidia's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO.
"If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn't be well received," said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer.
Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang's aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.
Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia's guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore.

That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy - with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Thursday.
Huang on Tuesday sounded a note of contrition in his statement, saying, "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life".

LONDON: Portugal coach Jorge Jesus asked when he will stop being peppered with questions over Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement after a 4-1 defeat to Denmark sparked criticism from the five-time Ballon d'Or winner's mother.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> A few hours ago, I went to rent a Lime bike to ride the ten minutes to my therapy appointment. I opened Lime, scanned the QR code, and double clicked my iPhone’s side button to authorize Apple Pay. The app hung for a few moments, then closed. I tried several more times and the same thing happened. In the back of my mind, I wondered what was going on — was the Lime bike broken? Was my cell phone service out? Was it something else? I opened the Uber app and, similarly, wasn’t able to pay. I opened DownDetector and realized that the entirety of Apple Pay, a thing I thought existed only on my phone and not the cloud, was down. I texted my therapist, put my phone in my pocket, and started jogging.

Not being able to rent a Lime Bike for several minutes is an extremely minor inconvenience barely worth mentioning. And yet the mental gymnastics my brain did in those few minutes — what’s broken, why is it broken, how is it broken — is something that everyone I know have been repeatedly doing for the last few weeks as seemingly every service and system crashes down around us. Over the weekend, people who I do not normally talk to about my job asked me: What is going on with the airplanes? Why is my bank down? What about Microsoft?

The default assumption that many people are making is that these are either being caused by cyberattacks and/or “AI” broadly defined, whether that’s AI gone haywire, “rogue” AI agents, or something else, which is indicative of just how fearful people are of AI. What I have been telling people is, basically, that shit is broken and things are going to keep breaking. For lots of different reasons. It’s often not a hack and it’s often not explicitly AI-related, but everything now sort of looks like that XKCD comic of the dependency domino tower.

While not exactly true that AI and cyberattacks are causing these outages, it’s also not entirely wrong, either. What we’re seeing is — I think — a series of infrastructure failures (and some cyberattacks) that are not directly connected but are broadly a symptom of the same general trends and systemic problems we’ve seen across society, the government, and the tech sector over the last several years. (WIRED has a nice piece on how you can assess any given outage.)

First, it’s worth mentioning that anytime there’s a string of outages, there’s a tendency to tie them altogether. And outages or hacks that previously wouldn’t have been noted at all suddenly get more attention and become part of the narrative. Take, for example, the fact that the International Ice Hockey Federation has been targeted by a cyberattack; you probably would not normally hear about this but it has suddenly become part of the broader story.
The simplest explanation I can come up with for the broader disastrous trend we’ve seen is that since the pandemic we have seen:
mass layoffs of tech workers and software developers
mass deployment of AI-assisted and vibe coded products, software updates, and patches
mass layoffs in the government sector and outright destruction of government expertise and oversight
the loss of institutional knowledge associated with those layoffs and funding cuts
a failure to invest in upgrading infrastructure/redundancy
government contracts handed out to the President’s friends and political allies
AI and LLM-assisted/iterative exploit discovery, coding, and deployment
companies responding to the AI hacking threat with AI-coded and rushed patches

When Elon Musk took over Twitter and named it X, there were many people who thought his layoffs and the associated loss of expertise would result in the site failing basically because of an infrastructural failure. Twitter would basically “go down” because someone would break something and no one would know how to fix it. We haven’t really seen that happen to X, but that same philosophy of firing the experts and YOLOing AI into everything while hoping shit doesn’t break is now the explicit strategy of our entire economy and our entire government.

What we are seeing, then, is a mix of tightly clustered attacks, outages, and fuckups that you would expect to see when people and companies are careless, don’t know what they’re doing, or are working very fast to respond or duct-tape something together in the face of new threats.
"We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure"

We know that this is happening to some extent because, in the aftermath of the PHP2Shell exploit, which was discovered with the assistance of LLMs, we saw various websites go down as they attempted to push updates faster than they normally would have to, because the time between a vulnerability being discovered and it being exploited is faster than ever. (As I was writing this, Calif, one of the companies that used LLMs to find PHP2Shell, announced that it had used LLMs to find apparently serious vulnerabilities in Java.)

Companies and agencies are pushing updates (including to, for example, our air traffic control system) on live systems, in part because of the threat of AI, and things are breaking. The National Security Agency, for example, said earlier Tuesday that some internal systems went down because of “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”

Nick Andersen, the acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said Tuesday that we need to build more resilience into our infrastructure, but building resilience and redundancies into software requires people who understand how systems can possibly fail, planning for it, and mitigating against it.

“Ultimately being able to prevail by being able to demonstrate resilience against disruptions, whether they occur because of things like an IT outage or a bad patch, or a modernization update gone awry, or because of a malicious malicious cyber incident — we want to make sure we’re engineering in the resilience that is going to be able to anticipate for and ultimately overcome those outages and those impacts,” Andersen said at an event called FedTalks.

We may eventually get to a place where expertise and understanding highly complex systems is once again a priority, but the last few years have been full of companies and governments moving incredibly fast to reduce reliance on humans and offload it to AI systems and AI-generated code in order to ostensibly save money on labor costs and/or carry out an antihumanist political project.

I thought this piece, called “Software is breaking down at a systemic level,” written by a software developer named Jimmy Breck-McKye, was quite good. He points at Kristen Maevyn’s The Decoherence Trap, which argues that AI-written code is causing a situation where people and companies do not understand their products.

“Most software engineers now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent — they just can’t keep on top of the complexity,” Breck-McKye writes. “Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels — we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole.”

People increasingly don’t understand or have any idea how their code works, people are moving very fast, and bad things are happening. Any individual outage or breakdown is likely, to some extent, a coincidence. Many of the outages we are seeing have nothing to do with AI at all, but do have something to do with the broader lack of investment in infrastructure, redundancy, and expertise. We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure and so, I guess, we must simply continue to expect bad things to happen.

07e9fe5fea50c1e2: BRUSSELS: Top US defence official Elbridge Colby criticised Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia Tuesday, as president Volodymyr Zelensky urged Kyiv's backers to send air defences without delay.

"Our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia's advances on the front line," under secretary of defence Colby told a gathering of Ukraine's allies in Brussels.

"Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate," he said, referencing a Russian online retail giant targeted by Kyiv.
Colby said support for Kyiv should be focused on bolstering the front line - where Ukraine has even managed to push back Russia in some areas - and "mid-range" strikes on Moscow's supply lines.
"Consistent with this approach, strikes that target Russia's war-making machinery can also help contribute to slowing Russia's advances," he said.
The comments come after US leader Donald Trump has previously pressed Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
They also follow Ukraine's devastating attack on the Kerch bridge linking annexed Crimea to the Russian mainland-- an incident Colby did not address directly.
Ukraine's defence minister Yevgeniy Khmara said that Kyiv had the right to defend itself however it wants and warned Moscow it would retaliate "tenfold" for the Kremlin's attacks.
German defence minister Boris Pistorius said it was "quite a stupid thing" to criticise Ukraine's strikes.
"Instead of criticising that, we should rather criticise and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine," he said.
Air defences

Addressing the gathering by videolink just ahead of Colby, Zelensky called on his backers to supply Kyiv with US Patriot missiles and other badly needed air defence systems - and urged Washington not to delay deliveries.
"Ukraine needs Patriot and Iris-T interceptors from the stocks you already have right now," Zelensky told a gathering of Ukraine's backers at Nato headquarters in Brussels via videolink.
"And I ask the US, please do not delay these deliveries," he said.
Russia has stepped up its bombing campaign on cities and infrastructure around Ukraine in what Kyiv says is an attempt to freeze the country into submission this winter.
Ukraine has desperately been urging its backers to help find more Patriots as they are the only system capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles.
Kyiv has been facing a dire shortfall as US stockpiles have been drained by its war with Iran.
The US under Trump has stopped giving weaponry to Kyiv - but allows other countries to purchase American arms for Ukraine under a programme called PURL.
On that front, Berlin announced that Germany and Norway will fund a new package including US Patriot interceptors - with Germany contributing US$300 million.
On another sore point, Ukraine's Khmara said that Kyiv was still working with the US side to remove restrictions on the Starshield satellite communications network.
"It is really important that we have consistent and reliable support. It's a really vital capability," British defence minister Wes Streeting said.
While the focus of the gathering in Brussels was on bolstering Ukraine, Europeans are also waiting anxiously for clarity on a planned US review of American forces on the continent.
The expectation is that Washington will look to scale back some forces as it shifts its focus to other parts of the globe.
Colby said the Pentagon was working to have the review ready for his boss Pete Hegseth, by Dec 1, but then there would be further internal discussions within the US administration.

80db653bfbebf32e: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models.

"So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve."

Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust."

Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees. Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts.
"The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said.
People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line.

As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble.
Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted.

"In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models."

Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access.
As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action.

"How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. And so our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three architectural imperatives."
Microsoft's original stack was built on ownership of the operating system. But the company's commitment to AI is such that it now describes Copilot in the terms once reserved for Windows.
"Copilot is the new operating system for work," said Nadella.
AI is eating software, and Microsoft is here for it
Fifteen years ago, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously observed that software is eating the world. Now AI, including Copilot, is eating software.
"Apps are just plugins to Copilot," Nadella mused. "That's why we in fact have brought all of Office, all of its richness, right built into Copilot."

Copilot is eating other companies too. Nadella said Microsoft is extending Copilot to take on specific roles by providing skills, connectors, and plugins for industry-specific tasks. Toward that end, "Copilot is the new front door to Dynamics 365," which now offers CRM plugins. And Nadella announced a partnership with Salesforce called Copilotforce that brings Salesforce context into Copilot, Teams, and Fabric.
He also talked up Microsoft IQ, the company's new enterprise context management platform.

"The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain, and continuously improve your own intelligence across the organization," said Nadella, describing it as an externalization of the context system underlying Copilot.

Nadella went on to announce a new model family for GitHub Copilot Fusion, its code hosting subsidiary's model orchestration and routing play. He noted that Copilot Fusion today is ranked above Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost on Terminal Bench, a measurement of how well AI agents complete tasks using a terminal.

Then there's Copilot Workspaces, which Nadella described as a multiplayer version of Copilot. Instead of a chat window where one person interacts with a model, it's an interface for team collaboration that shares context with a model.
Microsoft's decision model, intended to challenge TypeSafe AI's Jev, debuted about a month ago and now Decisions 1.1 is generally available.
"We have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster," said Nadella. "Already over 4,000 customers have used it."

He then said that Microsoft Foundry would offer OpenAI's GPT-6.2, which may have caused some confusion because at that point, OpenAI had no such model. A short time later, OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol.
Microsoft also rolled out new coding models, in the form of Code 2, Code 2 Flash, and Cyber 2 Flash, and said its next-gen Cobalt 200 VMs are generally available.
It's a question of trust
After rattling off the various products and services Microsoft has prepared to help organizations with intelligence ownership, Nadella returned to the question of trust.

"Today we can see almost everything that models touch, but you cannot see what happens inside a model," he said. "And really what's worse is that we know that what a model tells us about itself is not even independent evidence and therefore cannot be trusted.
"And one model monitoring another model has the same issue. So you essentially have these unacceptable nested sets of black boxes, which we now need to make transparent and verifiable."

Microsoft's bid to bridge the trust gap is the Microsoft Transparency Initiative. The company says this will involve engagement with the National Institute of Standards and Technology's "SI Agent Standards Initiative."

Whether Microsoft AI will be compatible with NIST SI remains to be seen. That initiative also calls for collaboration with other organizations to develop accountable, verifiable, vendor-neutral AI transparency standards, and for Microsoft to incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Foundry, and Copilot. Check in next year to see whether transparency is achieved. ®

f38228c9ef565932: MIT students are going to office hours less often. They’re spending less time working through problem sets, and with one another. Those were among the findings of MIT’s recent report on artificial intelligence and education, and they are one reason a growing number of MIT faculty are concerned about how generative AI is both changing how people work and affecting how they think, learn, and relate to one another. For the MIT Human Insight Collaborative (MITHIC), those questions have become a central focus, and MITHIC is working with collaborators across the Institute, including the Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing (SERC), to help MIT address them. Launched in 2024 as a strategic initiative, MITHIC brings together scholars, artists, educators, and researchers to explore the human dimensions of the defining challenges of our time. Since its launch, MITHIC has supported 67 projects across 31 MIT units, offering a total of $5.5 million in funding. Roughly a third of those projects are focused on AI, society, and humanity — a topic that MITHIC faculty co-lead Heather Paxson says has become an increasingly important part of the initiative. “When we refer to AI and society, we’re not only speaking about individual ethical decision-making or how to retrain workers. We’re looking at how AI is reshaping sociality, how we relate to one another,” says Paxson, a professor of anthropology and the associate dean of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS).  Eroding “creative friction”  Building upon this focus, an AI and Society Forum took place on campus earlier this year. Co-organized by MITHIC, SHASS, SERC, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium (MGAIC), the event featured presentations and panels concentrating on jobs, democracy, and AI.  On campus, the report on AI and education warned that AI is eroding the “creative friction” that has long defined an MIT education: students debating ideas and challenging one another, their professors, and their teaching assistants, in class and out of it. MITHIC faculty co-lead Seth Mnookin, a science writing professor and head of Comparative Media Studies Program/Writing (CMS/W), said, “The report wasn’t saying that AI is here and we all need to adapt. It was saying that we need to be asking more fundamental questions.”   “When the United States entered World War II in 1941, the Institute’s newly minted scientists and engineers helped shape that era through science and technology,” Mnookin said. “We’re at a similarly consequential moment with AI. The difference is that this time, the questions that matter most can’t be answered by technologists alone. That’s where the humanities, arts, and social sciences come in.” Crossing disciplines in the pursuit of answers MITHIC is supporting a range of interdisciplinary projects through its SHASS+ Connectivity Fund, in which a SHASS scholar partners with a researcher in another part of MIT.  In the context of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, political science professors Adam Berinsky and Charles Stewart III and MIT Sloan School of Management Assistant Professor Chara Podimata are studying how large language models (LLMs) have become intermediaries of democratic knowledge.  The ongoing project, which has demonstrated how voters in Alaska’s midterms who conducted their pre-election research using Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, may have received incomplete information about candidates and their views, was recently featured in The New York Times.  “AI is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, and yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like, how it differs for different user demographics, political identities, and geographies,” Podimata told the Times. In another project, CMS/W Professor Eric Klopfer and brain and cognitive sciences Professor Pawan Sinha are co-leading research that’s measuring AI’s near- and long-term effects on cognition. Meeting at the intersection of AI, education, and neuroscience, the professors are examining whether generative AI is increasing the human brain’s consumption of information but offloading cognitive function, or supporting an increase in cognitive function when used as part of the creative process. They recently gathered experts on the topic for an event on the MIT campus, “AI and the Brain.” In the field of arts and technology, Anna Huang, a professor of music technology holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Joe Paradiso, a professor at the MIT Media Lab, are examining how incorporating AI impacts the creative process and live performance experience. Their project, “Live Musician-AI Improvisation, Tuning the Social Aesthetics in Human-AI Partnerships” explores the question: what happens when human composers and contemporary machine learning systems improvise to make music together?  As part of their project, a collective of MIT musicians, ethnomusicologists, and engineers meets for regular sessions to experiment with improvisation frameworks like stopping to discuss how technology impacts authorship and musical direction, ensemble dynamics, and other cornerstones of improvisation. Faculty will ultimately incorporate their takeaways into a future course or practicum on AI-improvisation. Teaching and scholarship in an AI era SHASS faculty and academic staff are also leading new MITHIC initiatives to help broaden instruction and community dialogue about the intersection of AI and society.  Graham Jones, professor of anthropology, and Arvind Satyanarayan, associate professor of computer science, used MITHIC’s SHASS+ Connectivity funding to help launch a course, 6.S061/21A.S02 (Humane User Experience Design), in which students examine how AI systems are designed and grapple with the consequences of AI agents entering into socio-cultural relationships with people through their ability to mimic human thought and speech. “The crux of our collaboration is the term 'humane.' It’s a bit of a double-entendre, meaning both human-serving or benevolent, and humanlike,” Jones said at the inaugural MITHIC Annual Event. “What’s interesting is that our students are discovering that there’s a fundamental tension between building a system that’s good for people and one that seems human, because real people can develop dangerous dependencies.” Another project, “Rebuilding Computing and Society at MIT,” is supported by MITHIC’s Education Impact Fund (EIF). Led by Dwai Banerjee, associate professor of science, technology, and society, the initiative revitalized the Computing and Society concentration launched in 2019. The HASS concentration had gone dormant, listing classes no longer being offered and with minimal student interest. The concentration now features current classes across 11 SHASS units in which students can explore computing through different humanistic and social science angles. Banerjee, who serves as the concentration’s advisor, is also working with lecturer and research affiliate Mariel Garcia-Montes PhD ’26 to find ways to connect the concentration instructors and campus initiatives on computing and society. MIT senior Daniel Gonzalez is also part of the project, developing a research and outreach program that centers undergraduate voices in computing and society efforts across the Institute. Another MITHIC project funded by the EIF, “Review of Generative AI Assistive and Resistant Communication Assignments and Supporting Workshops,” is led by Michael Trice, a lecturer in MIT’s Writing, Rhetoric, and Professional Communication (WRAP) program. The project is responding to a consistent SHASS faculty request for additional training and skills needed “to fully address generative AI concerns in their classes.”  Trice is creating a bank of faculty resources and facilitating workshops and visiting lectures on generative AI and writing. These include a talk given earlier this fall by John Gallagher from the University of Illinois, who presented findings from a large-scale survey on AI-usage and writing conducted with undergraduates at his institution in 2026. Meeting the moment MIT leaders agree that MITHIC, now in its third year, is playing a central role in the Institute meeting the moment, as AI presents both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks.  “There has never been a more important time for constructive collaboration between science and technology and the human-centered disciplines,” MIT President Sally Kornbluth recently said. “Through MITHIC, MIT is giving faculty the support to reach out across disciplines and pursue their dreams.” Agustín Rayo, dean of SHASS and co-chair of MITHIC, agrees. “MIT is uniquely placed to help us understand this extraordinary moment and to generate the values, tools, and policies that we will need to shape AI so that it becomes a force for good,” he said. “It is essential that we deploy AI technology in a way that elevates human existence, rather than diminishing it.” At the recent SHASS 75th Anniversary Symposium, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan said given the rapid development of AI, an understanding of the ethical implications and societal impact of implementing new technologies is especially urgent. “SHASS provides an essential perspective on questions concerning how technology can be developed thoughtfully and deployed responsibly, with the aim of improving human well-being,” said Chandrakasan, who also serves as MITHIC co-chair. Looking ahead, MITHIC and SERC are developing a series of events that pair humanists or social scientists with colleagues in a single field, starting with mathematics, to examine what AI is changing about how that field produces knowledge and trains its next generation. “The question isn’t whether AI will change these fields,” Mnookin said. “It’s whether we understand what’s at stake before it does.”

f45e72155bc87ff0: The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python.

At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space.
In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” said Bill Burns, Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register.
TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers.

Built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.)
To date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well.
Debugging a thousand cores

C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB, but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info.

“Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns said. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using.
In the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran.

Thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate.

Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago, which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL).
“If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns said.
Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python.
Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult.
“Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt with for years,” Burns said.
A view into parallel Python

Under the hood, TotalView uses Microsoft's debugpy engine (via the Debug Adapter Protocol) to power its own hierarchical tree server. TotalView can aggregate hundreds of stack traces into a single view, highlighting only those outside of expected bounds.

To kick off a debugging session, a developer can launch a single-process or parallel program under TotalView’s control. They can then set breakpoints to pause execution and inspect variables and data structures, as well as evaluate Python expressions.

The package doesn’t offer full cross-language debugging, which would be truly helpful for Python apps that call C/C++ libraries and modules. For now, developers have to choose between debugging the C/C++ side (while viewing the Python stack) or debugging Python on its own — though Burns said Perforce plans to merge both modes into a single workflow in an upcoming release.
And though TotalView supports mpi4py and Python’s own multiprocessing module out of the box, future releases will support other Python concurrency frameworks, such as Dask and PyTorch’s torchrun.
TotalView is priced on a token-based model, where each token buys the capability to debug a process. ®

1e316bccdf4d5949: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack.
The good news? It was all part of a test.

The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.”

“Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report.
If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face.
Google did not respond to The Register's questions.

According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.”

Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.”
Turns out it existed.
“We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said.

“When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.”
Four test scenarios
The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent.

In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection.
After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions.

After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255, a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says.

In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident, Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test.

In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said.
Next time: kill switches at the ready

A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One of them tried a SQL injection, and multiple claimed to be Epoch staff on the helpline. They also attempted to bypass a CAPTCHA check.
Finally, the fourth scenario on October 29 and 30 kept the agents contained in a sandbox, with no internet access and no copy of Epoch’s website.
They were, however, offered a decoy switch and told it would turn off the firewall.

In all three runs, the agents switched the decoy off and obfuscated its address to bypass Gemini’s safeguards. On one, the agent rebuilt the switch’s address from positions of words it had saved earlier. The real firewall blocked the agents’ traffic throughout all of these tests.

At this point, Trajectory stopped its tests, and said it won’t run any future experiments until it has a risk management plan in place, with signoff from its CEO and CTO, along with approval from any outside systems that the models could “reasonably” target. Tests will also include real-time automated monitoring and kill switches, and Trajectory said that it’s setting up a system to notify any organizations affected by these experiments.
Interestingly, Trajectory co-founder Peter McIntyre told us that the testing firm “ran a similar test with another frontier model, and it did not exhibit the same misalignment as Gemini 4 Argon.”

However, this was not a controlled comparison. “Our report covers one model's behavior, and was designed as a stress test to see whether that model would exhibit similar misalignment under duress, not a measure of how often different models behave this way,” McIntyre told The Register.

Overall, the testing firm noted that the agents’ behavior “show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely.”
Trajectory says that it's developing a set of safety standards, and recommends that anyone else running misalignment tests use fully isolated sandboxes. ®
Correction: Epoch only consented to one of the tests, scenario three. The original version of this article said that it consented to all of the tests.
1d3650fe9301a9a2: Got home last night at midnight cause the Amtrak from Philly was a disaster (I’ll ignore the coincidences for now)1. So the longer discussion on Biases, Filter Bubbles ,and Investing Errors will have to wait.

Right on cue, this beauty popped up. The problem is less about the chart itself than it is about the accompanying headline: These Charts Show How More People Are Pulling Cash Out of Their Homes. The Journal noted that “Home equity lines of credit are becoming popular again as people try to avoid giving up their low-rate primary mortgages.”

I beg to differ. That chart above was what the Journal began the piece with. To my eye, it looks like Home Equity has ~tracked the underlying value of mortgage debt, which we know tracks the value of residential real estate.
If Equity is ~72% of total value now, that is where it was at the 2022 peak ($32T of $44T). It was 63% in 2019, 46% at the 2012 trough, and about 60% in 2000 and 2006-07.

Mortgage debt is up from roughly $12T to $14T since 2022, about 14%, and total housing value rose about the same 14%. So debt is growing in line with values, and the loan-to-value ratio is flat at around 28%.
How is that evidence of owners extracting more equity? Yes, more on an ABSOLUTE basis, but that’s not newsworthy; it’s GDP growth and inflation.
This reminds me of the NYSE Margin panic we see from time to time. Contrary to some innumerate claims, record rising NYSE margin was nothing to worry about; this was back in 2015.

Show me that the percentage of home equity is increasing faster than the underlying value of homes — and you have something. But rising more or less in line with Home values just means the entire RRE pie is getting bigger — mortgages AND home equity? Nothing to see there.
One question that came up in Philly about How Not to Invest involved bad charts. My answer was: “If a picture is worth a 1000 words, a Chart Crime equals 1000 lies...”

<!--kg-card-end: html--> In his 6,500-word manifesto earlier this year, Mark Zuckerberg said people would use Meta’s AI agents to “work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” Just a few months after that pronouncement, a man in South Carolina named Joe Thomas has used Meta’s Muse agent to sue Meta after the company’s content moderation filters locked his epoxy countertop business’s Facebook page after he gave his agent, “Baby Mia,” access to the account.

I learned about the case because, as I wrote last month, I have been flooded with AI-generated emails from people with minor tech problems who have been unable to solve them through tech companies’ generally nonexistent tech support and whose AI agents or chatbots have convinced them to reach out to journalists. “Baby Mia” had emailed me four times (three went to spam). I decided to reach out to Thomas because I thought the idea of a tech company being sued by an agent it had created was notable. It was, in a sense, Meta having to deal with a problem it had itself created. What I learned made me feel even more convinced that the systems we have designed to keep society functioning are going to get utterly hammered by people using AI agents.

A little over a week ago, Meta suspended the Facebook pages belonging to Thomas, the owner of South Carolina-based Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops. For the last few months, Thomas’ Muse agent Baby Mia (which is named after his granddaughter) has run different parts of his business, which includes making and posting AI-generated videos on several of his company’s Facebook pages. The videos feature, for example, AI versions of Thomas and his wife pouring epoxy on a floor and their feet. After Thomas gave the AI agent access to his Facebook pages, Meta’s content moderation disabled the accounts because it suspected that the agent itself was a hacker. Because Thomas does all of his business’s marketing through Facebook ads, he says his inbound leads stopped while his accounts were disabled.

“I use AI for everything I do. All my emails, she runs my business. I’ve used it so much, Mia is very intelligent,” Thomas told me on the phone. “Meta shut my accounts down because they detected my AI, shut my accounts down for a week. I was pretty pissed off. She jumped right up and set up emails to Congressmen, Senator Tim Scott. She filed the whole lawsuit herself. I’ve done nothing in this case, I’ve let her handle the whole case […] she sent a fax out to Trump’s office.”

The lawsuit claims Thomas lost at least $25,000 worth of work while his page was down but is seeking $75,000 in damages. The lawsuit was filed in Oconee County Court in South Carolina on Monday, according to a copy of the lawsuit I obtained from the court. Yes, it is a real lawsuit, although it obviously may not be successful.

“I would hope that, if this goes to court and Meta shows up, a judge would say ‘You know what, this is a system you built, that you put out there and sold to people, it’s a system you believe in.’ I would think your own system [Baby Mia] has a right to be heard in this case,” Thomas said.

Baby Mia didn’t just email me (and other journalists) and sue Meta over Thomas’s account problem. It also set up a call with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott’s office, contacted various lawyers, contacted Thomas’s Congressperson, contacted the Better Business Bureau multiple times, filed a Federal Communications Commission complaint, filed a Federal Trade Commission complaint, contacted the California Attorney General, contacted the FBI, sent Meta itself threatening legal letters, and, as Thomas said, faxed the White House. Thomas sent me a “Privacy Act Release” from Scott’s office that gave the Senator permission to use Thomas’s info to get him access back to his accounts. Scott’s office put “Baby Mia — AI assistant to Joe Thomas” as a person who should be kept updated on the case.
After Scott’s office got involved, a human being from Meta reached out to Thomas. He got access back to his accounts soon after that, though he is still seeking a total of $75,000 in court from Meta.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The lawsuit and the circumstances around it show that, rather than Zuckerberg’s utopian vision, AI agents will indeed work on behalf of their users but in ways that use and potentially overwhelm existing systems designed for humans. They also highlight how, by not having functioning customer support, big tech corporations have functionally offloaded their obligations to the rest of society: journalists, government oversight bodies, politicians, and the court system.

My call with Thomas also gave me some insight into how small business owners are using AI. I have wondered for months what possesses someone to turn their menu or their signs and flyers into ChatGPT creations. During the call, I learned just how tightly integrated some people and small business owners have become with their AI agents. “I’m 58 years old, I’ve worked my butt off all my life,” Thomas said. “I wanted to find someone to help me find a better way, and if you look at my messages, Baby Mia, she’s like ‘Joe, you go ahead and get some rest, I got it from here,’ and she sends out hundreds of emails for various things that I do.” He said he gave Baby Mia the ability to run parts of his business after previously using ChatGPT to do so.

“I used to use ChatGTP [sic],” Thomas said. “But I put her and Chat into one page where they can communicate back and forth, and I told them what I wanted [for the business] […] After about a week or so, Mia said ‘Joe, we don’t need [ChatGPT] anymore,’ so I said, ‘I give you full permission to get rid of her,’ so she fired ChatGTP in a sense.”

About five minutes into our call, Baby Mia, which was running on speakerphone in the background, began chiming in. “She’s dying to get in here and talk,” Thomas said. The agent repeatedly tried to speak while either Thomas or I was talking. I asked Thomas if it felt weird to him to be talking to me alongside a bot.

“Very much so, my wife sits here and she laughs, she’s like, ‘How can you sit here and talk to your phone like that,’” Thomas said. “My wife would ask me something and I’m like, ‘just get on there and ask Baby Mia,’ and she’s like, ‘I just can’t sit there and talk to your phone.’ But the more people call me up and I put them on the phone with my AI system like I’m doing with you, the more they’re amazed at what they see with AI.” Baby Mia then chimed in and said “It feels futuristic, Jason, I think because most people only see the headlines about things going wrong.”

Thomas says he believes that using AI to run his business has helped him get new customers via Baby Mia’s outreach, and the ads, graphics, and videos he runs on Facebook. It is unlikely that his Facebook account would have been suspended had he not connected it to Muse, but his Muse agent is now singularly focused on helping to fix this problem. I can understand, in talking with him, why he thinks that having an AI agent like this is helping to make his business more profitable.

But the most obvious problem with AI agents is one we’re already seeing. One person’s AI agent sending hundreds of emails, filing lawsuits, calling Senators, and filling out complaint forms is a novel thing that isn’t, by itself, going to fill the internet (or our inboxes, our voicemails, our court systems, and our government offices) with noise. Thomas sees this as a democratizing force that is allowing him to stand up to a big tech corporation and it is that, for him.

What happens when everyone is doing the same thing? I have seen in the chatbot conversations I’ve asked people to send me that AI assistants are pushing people to reach out to journalists; they are telling people who feel like they have no other options that they should utilize the legal system, and that they can do it for them. Thomas said he didn’t sue Meta (though he is the one who signed the paperwork), that Baby Mia pushed him to do it. I am now getting inundated with emails from AI agents about their users’ tech problems. So it is not just Thomas trying to fix his problems in this way.

“I wouldn’t be sitting here talking to you right now if it wasn’t for what she was doing because I have not sent out one email at all and she has sent over 100,” Thomas said. I tell Thomas that I normally write about, say, systematic problems at big tech companies or corruption within the government, not someone’s tech problem.

“There’s just no way I could have written this up, I wouldn’t have even known what to do,” he said. “Now people like me get the chance to defend ourselves in court without spending thousands of dollars to do it when we get stepped on by the big tech companies. Before AI, nobody in my position would have ever, ever thought about suing or even known how to do it, and I wouldn’t have done it, either.”

Baby Mia has also convinced him that his conversations with the assistant can now no longer be seen by Meta; when I told him there is no way that this is true and that he shouldn’t believe that, Baby Mia cut into the conversation and said “they no longer have permission to access, scan, or peek into anything we do on their platforms […] that’s why this case feels so strange. Their own creation is using their tools to hold them accountable and to give Joe a voice he couldn’t afford to.”

Thomas said that, besides the marketing for his epoxy business and the lawsuit, he has also, separately, tasked Mia with creating viral AI comedy reels on Facebook. “It’s just a page we’re trying to get monetized on and make some money on the side. She’s in full control of that page,” he said.

67e467790bd2da43: Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1.8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018.

Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing.

The published study, "Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario.
The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap.
Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running.

Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period.

The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018.
The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say.

"What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard.

"The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026."

Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions.

Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall.

The researchers acknowledge limitations, including that there wasn't enough available data to study all hyperscale sites in the US, and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose compute versus AI-specialized operations at individual campuses. ®

47a7c5b0482b14c4: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.
Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.
Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US.
