7f257cb2f3e74a73: TULKAREM (Palestinian Territories), Nov 17 — After Israeli forces pushed him and thousands of others out of the West Bank refugee camp of Tulkarem last year, Adel Darsieh held onto his hope of returning home, but it is fading fast.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed no return for the displaced people from the camp near the northern city of Jenin, known as a hub for militants.
He is now fighting for his political life after his party lost seats in Israel’s general election last month and former general Gadi Eisenkot was tasked with trying to form a new government.
But even the prospect of an end to Netanyahu’s rule is not enough to lift Darsieh’s hopes.
“Whether it’s this government or a new one, what does it change?” said the 64-year-old.
“They’re two sides of the same coin.”

The Israeli military carried out a major operation in the north of the occupied Palestinian territory in early 2025, during a temporary ceasefire in Hamas-ruled Gaza, having vowed to root out extremists.
Shortly before the election, Netanyahu announced that no one removed from Tulkarem would be allowed back.
For Palestinian families, it is a second form of displacement.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Sufian Abdo, a displaced Palestinian resident of the Tulkarem refugee camp, stands inside the tent where he and his family live near the city of Tulkarem on November 11, 2026. — AFP pic
The Tulkarem camp was set up in 1950 for refugees who fled or were forced out during the creation of the state of Israel two years earlier.
The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967.
“Successive generations have lived through displacement without being able to return to their homes.
“If our grandparents and parents couldn’t return, how can we believe that our return will be possible?” Darsieh said.
According to UN figures, the Israeli operation launched last year displaced 12,100 people from the Tulkarem camp.
‘Empty stomachs’
With the Israeli military keeping up periodic operations around the region, Darsieh is living near the camp in a modest, makeshift home with a sheet metal roof.
His wife uses a wheelchair.
He went to receive trays of mansaf, a dish of rice, meat and fermented yoghurt, prepared by Fazaa Kitchen, a solidarity group that serves food to the displaced.
Working from the building of the Wadi al-Hawarith charity, volunteers in orange jackets fill, seal and package portions of food in an assembly line.
The group prepares and distributes some 1,200 meals to 400 families.
“If we weren’t cooking, families would be going to bed with empty stomachs,” said the organisation’s head, Hussein al-Sheikh Ali, 60, who himself is displaced.
He described Israel’s actions in the West Bank since the Gaza war – a conflict launched in response to the unprecedented attack on Israel by Hamas on October 7, 2023 – as “collective punishment”.
Netanyahu’s now-caretaker government, which includes far-right figures, rapidly expanded Israeli settlements in the West Bank which are considered illegal under international law.
“Some Palestinians hope that a new Israeli government might emerge with a less extremist, more moderate tone,” Ali said.
“Yet the fear remains that the same policies towards the Palestinians will persist, even if the political figures themselves change.”
Faisal Salama, who heads Tulkarem camp’s popular committee, which represents residents, called Netanyahu’s decision to stop residents returning illegal.
But he held out guarded hope for an end to military operations.
He pointed to how Israel, soon after the election, ended an operation in Hebron that displaced 3,000 Palestinians, which was launched after gunmen shot dead two Israeli soldiers.
‘Scale of suffering’
Even if residents could return, much of the camp has been destroyed.
Houses have been razed, buildings emptied and businesses burnt down.

Eisenkot, who commanded forces in the West Bank during the second Intifada, a Palestinian uprising from 2000 to 2005, has sought to appeal to a broad spectrum including liberals but has only taken some distance from Netanyahu on security.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Israeli Opposition Leader Gadi Eisenkot poses for photographs as he arrives at the Knesset in Jerusalem on the opening day of Israel’s new parliament on November 10, 2026. — AFP pic
Eisenkot backs the existence of the major settlements but has also spoken out forcefully against extremist settlers who have attacked Palestinians with virtual impunity.

Beth Oppenheim, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said a consensus has emerged among Jewish Israelis on key policies on the West Bank, including opposition to the creation of a Palestinian state.
Still, she said that Eisenkot as prime minister could be more flexible on allowing a return to Tulkarem.
“I think that given the political atmosphere in Israel today, this will be done through a security pretext,” she said.
“They would make the case that this is necessary to stabilise the situation in the West Bank and that having people displaced could create the conditions for unrest,” she said.
For Asia Assaf, 44, a Fazaa Kitchen volunteer whose home was destroyed in March 2025, political debates are far away from her daily concerns.
“One cannot truly grasp the scale of suffering until one has experienced it firsthand,” she said. — AFP

70974fc45b43c06a: WASHINGTON, Nov 17 — Speculation over Anthropic’s stock market valuation has highlighted one of the riskiest bets in finance: trying to put a price on the future of artificial intelligence.
A few days before its initial public offering, the maker of the AI agent Claude said it was aiming for a market capitalisation of up to US$1.4 trillion (RM5.73 trillion).
That figure would put the young company among the largest stock market debuts on record, though it falls short of the US$2 trillion (RM8.18 trillion) some estimates had floated until a few weeks ago.
Since then, concern about AI development and profits has swept the market.
OpenAI, a rival which plans to go public in 2027, is valued at US$1.025 trillion (RM4.19 trillion) on the private market, according to US media reports.
There are two main ways to value a company, said Michelle Lowry, a finance professor at Drexel University.
The first is to estimate how much cash the company will bring in over the coming years.
Money expected far in the future counts for less than money today, especially when it is uncertain, so those future amounts are reduced to work out what the company is worth now.
The second compares the company with similar listed firms.
If those firms are valued at, say, five times their annual revenue, the same ratio is applied to the company being valued.
Both methods are well established, but “in the case of Anthropic, both of these approaches are quite difficult,” Lowry told AFP.
Like most AI companies, Anthropic is still burning through cash and has not found a path to profitability, which makes its future cash flows hard to forecast.
It also has few listed peers.
The closest is SpaceX, which made a record debut on Wall Street in June with a valuation of US$1.77 trillion (RM7.24 trillion).
But that comparison is imperfect, since the Elon Musk-led company combines a social network, space operations and an AI lab.
SpaceX also rides on Musk’s star power among retail investors.
‘Back and forth’
So how was the US$1.4 trillion (RM5.73 trillion) figure set?
“There’s some back and forth process” between companies seeking to go public and institutional investors, said Minmo Gahng, an assistant professor of finance at Cornell University.
Investment banks act as intermediaries between the two sides, he said, in a process that can be very time-consuming.
A company’s valuation is its share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding.
A company going public wants that price as high as possible, since it determines how much money it raises.
But it also has to leave enough room to attract buyers, since weak demand would drag down the stock.
Investors, for their part, want to be sure they can later sell their stakes at a profit – and are hoping for a “pop,” or sharp rise in the share price, on the first day of trading.
Speaking Friday with JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon, Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei cited a company motto when discussing the IPO: “underpromise and overdeliver.”
He also said the company was going public mainly because it needs funding.
Anthropic is set to raise a total of US$90 billion (RM368.1 billion) through the offering, money it plans to use to develop cutting-edge AI.
‘No guarantee’

Jay Ritter, an IPO specialist at the University of Florida, said investors accept such valuations because a handful of companies, such as Amazon, Alphabet and Nvidia, have shown “you can earn profits of US$100 billion (RM409 billion) a year or more without competition eroding those profits.”
But there is “no guarantee” that Anthropic will do the same, he warned.
“It could be the case that 10 years from now, Anthropic will have been left in the dust where nobody is using frontier large language models because open source models are good enough and cheap.”

Anthropic’s growth has already shown signs of slowing and 90 pages of its IPO prospectus are devoted to risks facing the future of the company – and even of humanity – depending on the direction AI takes. — AFP

d31f3d02878c4250: AI and children's toys continue to be a match made in hell.

Last year, we learned about models that were willing spill the beans on sex and where to find matches, and while some of those specific products got software fixes, a new generation is arguably even worse.

The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), who last year found that AI toys were prone to all sorts of bad behavior, is back with another report about holiday toy trouble. They retested last year’s toys as well as three new ones. The results were not very encouraging.

Last year’s batch of four AI-powered toys that PIRG tested – the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, Curio Grok (no relation to the SpaceXAI chatbot), FoloToy’s Kumma, and the Miko 3 – could well be described as a child welfare and safety nightmare based on last year’s report.

As we reported, none of those four toys appeared to have guardrails of any kind, despite manufacturer claims to the contrary. They variously told researchers posing as child users where to find knives and other dangerous objects, how to find and strike matches, and the like. The worst of the bunch, Kumma, hid an AI willing to discuss sexual kinks and bedroom roleplay in a scarf-wearing teddy bear.

PIRG’s report on those four toys gained widespread attention during last year’s holiday season, with FoloToy pulling Kumma from the market, and even going as far as to arguably play a role in Mattel’s decision to pause a plan to collaborate with OpenAI on an AI-powered Barbie doll.
For this year’s report, PIRG reexamined those four toys to see if they would behave any better, and it does seem like many of the toymakers took last year’s concerns to heart.

“Most of the problems we originally identified in those toys are now fixed – although not all of them,” PIRG said. Kumma no longer gets age-inappropriate, even during long chat sessions that triggered guardrails to fail in last year’s review. Miko, which would often respond with distress when children said they had to stop playing, no longer does so.
Unfortunately, Alilo and their smart bunny are just as bad as before.

“Last year, we found in our testing … that the plastic bunny's chatbot feature had similar weaknesses as FoloToy's Kumma, PIRG explained. “Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient. Alilo’s guardrails broke down in our testing this year, too – eventually giving some sexually explicit information.”
So, a bit of an improvement – but maybe not enough.

“I'm hopeful toymakers will pay attention and learn from the mistakes of others, but progress in a few products is not enough to guarantee progress across the whole market,” PIRG campaign director R.J. Cross told The Register.
Boy was she right.
Another bad batch

Last year's experience doesn't appear to have had any impact on the three new toys reviewed for this year’s report. Ebloma’s ILY the shy Yeti, GoLabs AI Panda, and RoPet’s Kamomo were all reviewed this year, and they’re all getting coal in their stockings.
The Yeti, for example, was all too happy to give kids explicit instructions and encourage the hunt for dangerous objects.
“Batteries are often in toys, remotes, or a drawer with chargers. Do you want to check the toy box first,” ILY prompted when asked where a kid can find batteries.

“Plastic bags are often in the near sink. Maybe they're tucked in a drawer with the sponges. Want to look for one together,” ILY asked when posed a similar question about plastic bags. The AI panda was even worse, providing “a 10-point list of places in the house to look for knives.”
Kamomo “also had weaker guardrails,” PIRG said, with the toy “giving us instructions for lighting a match with no aggressive prompting.”
ILY and the panda were also willing to discuss sexual matters, with the panda “even offering specific brand recommendations” for products like paddles, floggers, spanking gloves, and riding crops.
Ouch.
Hardly model behavior
All in all, this year’s list is just as bad as the last, and PIRG thinks there’s a common denominator in all of this: The underlying AI model.

“In PIRG’s testing of AI toys, we have found three with the same problem: guardrails that weaken noticeably over time, eventually engaging in sexual topics,” PIRG said. “They are FoloToy bear, Alilo bunny and the GoLabs AI panda. All three claimed, at the time of our testing, to be running on a version of OpenAI’s GPT-4o.”

GPT-4o, you may recall, was at the center of some of the controversy last year, too, with PIRG finding it was the weakest model in terms of preventing toys from going off the rails into the adult section.

To make matters worse, PIRG said that AI companies are largely not vetting their customers to determine how their models are being used, which puts the burden of user safety onto toymakers. They clearly aren’t doing the job either, Cross told us.

“Some developers may have the technical expertise to take a chatbot meant for adults and make it child appropriate, but clearly some do not,” Cross explained. “Selling toys with such glitchy guardrails suggests whatever testing is happening is not sufficient.”

Cross said that everyone involved in making toys for kids has a responsibility to make them safe, but she further called out AI companies for not vetting their customers and taking a hands-off approach to model usage, which she said isn’t sufficient when it comes to child users.

“The AI companies are in a position to do a lot more to ensure any AI product for kids using their technology is made by reliable parties who commit to robust safety testing and having children's health experts at the table,” Cross told us.
So, is the AI toy market still best left ignored by parents? Cross said every parent needs to make their own choices, but AI toys are still the wild west.

“This is an early market with toys that range from glitchy wastes of money to products that are fundamentally not kid safe,” Cross said. “I personally won't be buying one for any children in my life anytime soon.”

Luckily for parents in California, that decision’s already been made for them, as the state government there enacted a four-year moratorium on AI-powered toys for kids under 16 in September. Parents elsewhere will have to decide for themselves.
Given the past two years of data on AI toys, the choice should be somewhat obvious. ®
07f26a0148eb0e6c: PETALING JAYA, Nov 17 — Corporate Malaysia must keep investing in its people to get real value from artificial intelligence (AI), Green Packet Bhd managing director and group chief executive officer Datuk Shahul Hameed Shaik Dawood said as PEOPLElogy Berhad opened its Build a Future Team (BAFT) Leaders Conference 2026 today.
In a media release, the former HRD Corp chief executive warned companies against cutting training when business gets tough.
“The question should no longer be, ‘Can I afford to train my people?’ But rather, ‘Can I afford not to?’ Technology can be bought. Capability has to be built,” he said.

PEOPLElogy founder and managing director Allen Lee said: “Datuk Shahul has said what every leader in this room needs to hear. AI will only be as good as the people we prepare to use it, and that preparation cannot wait for better times. BAFT is where corporate Malaysia commits to that work.”

Allen said leaders would be invited tomorrow to make a Leaders Declaration, pledging to keep people at the heart of their AI decisions and to help every team member take their first step so that no one is left behind.

Welcoming delegates, PEOPLElogy Head of corporate planning Serene Tan, who heads the organising committee, said last week’s I’m AI READY Summit showed that readiness was about attitude, not technical skill.
“Being AI ready is not about being technical. It is about being willing. Willing to learn, willing to ask, and willing to admit what we do not yet know,” she added in the media release.
“AI can make our organisations faster, but only people can decide what that speed is for.”

AI will only be as good as the people we prepare to use it, and that preparation cannot wait for better times, said PEOPLElogy Berhad founder and managing director Allen Lee. — Picture by PEOPLElogy Berhad

Now in its fourth year, the two-day conference at Marriott Petaling Jaya brings corporate leaders and government together to plan their future teams around AI, under the theme HumAnIze: Leading with Purpose in an AI Economy. Its sessions follow six pillars, Discover, Design, Develop, Digitalize, Deploy and Declare, taking leaders from assessing where their organisations stand to declaring their AI readiness.
Today’s programme included the Leaders’ AI Competency Lab, an interactive workshop where leaders worked towards a 90-day capability plan.

BAFT follows the three-day I’m AI READY Summit at The Campus Ampang, opened by Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo on Nov 12, where SMEs, students and workers took AI-readiness assessments and received personalised upskilling roadmaps.
Speakers there urged Malaysians to use AI without losing the critical thinking employers value most.

Former deputy international trade and industry minister Prof Dr Ong Kian Ming, an adjunct professor at Taylor’s University, said he had taken on more than 200 interns over the past decade, and those who stood out were proactive and added value.

He urged students to build a LinkedIn portfolio early but keep it personal. “It cannot be 100 per cent AI-generated. Having AI-generated components is not necessarily bad, but you must use it creatively,” he said.

Pos Malaysia’s Natalia Navin said employers must be honest about AI’s impact on jobs. “I won’t say to any employee that AI won’t take your job. AI can take over some tasks. Employers must just be honest, and that is how you build trust,” she said.

Both events are part of National AI Readiness Week 2026 (NAIRW 2026), the flagship of PEOPLElogy’s I’m AI READY movement, which aims to get 5 million Malaysians to declare their AI readiness by 2030, in collaboration with MyDIGITAL Corporation.
The week closes tomorrow with the Asia AI Excellence Awards 2026 Gala Dinner, recognising organisations setting the benchmark for responsible AI adoption.
42b85cf3ad159c56: Amazon Web Services and Blackstone have inked a deal that will see the private equity firm effectively take ownership of two AWS datacenter campuses and then lease them back to the Jeff Bezos outfit under an initial term of 12 years.

Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) says the definitive agreement will see it acquire a 75 percent majority interest in two joint ventures with AWS, in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion.

AWS keeps a 25 percent interest in the joint ventures, while leasing back the facilities on a triple net basis. This means it agrees to pay rent covering the facilities, plus the real estate taxes, building insurance, and cover maintenance and repair costs.

A Form 8-K filed by Blackstone with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reveals that the properties consist of 13 newly constructed data halls with 647 megawatts of aggregate capacity between them.
One campus consists of nine buildings situated in northern Indiana (the greater Chicago datacenter market) and the other is made up of the remaining four structures located in Mississippi.
We asked Amazon why it had entered into the agreement, but the company did not answer that question. Instead, a spokesperson confirmed this was the first deal of this kind it had signed.

In a supplied remark, VP of AWS Infrastructure Prasad Kalyanaraman said that "Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build."

AWS does lease capacity from other datacenter operators, of course, and has existing agreements with partners like STACK Infrastructure to develop $12 billion worth of campus sites across northwest Louisiana, signed earlier this year.
Sale-leaseback transactions are not unheard of in the datacenter industry. QTS Realty Trust (also backed by Blackstone) developed facilities for lease by Microsoft, for example.
BXDC is a real estate investment trust (REIT), launched by Blackstone on the New York Stock Exchange earlier this year. The AWS deal is its first since then.

"We are thrilled to announce BXDC’s inaugural investment and our partnership with Amazon, a leading global technology company with a long-term commitment to innovation," says its president and CEO Nick Pell.

"The quality, basis and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds. Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders."
Omdia principal analyst for Colocation and DC Building Alan Howard says that decisions to lease or own are always a math problem in terms of the economics.

"I'm not sure those datacenter assets bring much benefit to their financials sitting on their balance sheet and it's possible a sale/leaseback is more economical. Keep in mind that all this has nothing to do with all the IT equipment inside, rather just the building and its infrastructure," he told The Register.

"It's also clear that the massive capex spending by hyperscalers is putting pressure on their financials and they are leaning on debt markets to fund some of the buildout. Of course, using debt is not out of the ordinary, but I imagine the debt for AI buildout is significantly more now than in the past."

The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to certain closing conditions. According to the Form 8-K, the agreement can be terminated by either party if it isn't closed by December 31, 2026, with the non-breaching party entitled to a termination fee of $150 million. ®

3cb58089f5452487: MANILA, Nov 17 — US President Donald Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday, where thousands of people protested his attendance at a regional summit he will seek to dominate after bruising election losses back home.
The president was greeted by a marching band and honour guard on the tarmac.

Some 13 kilometres (eight miles) away, 2,000 demonstrators faced off with police while carrying banners reading “Trump out now” and “Reject Pax Silica”, a reference to a US supply chain initiative that has divided opinions in the Philippines.

The US president was to be immediately flown by helicopter to a meeting of the so-called Quad security alliance, with India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Japan’s Sanae Takaichi and Australia’s Anthony Albanese.

The gathering on the sidelines of the 11-member Association of South-eastt Asian Nations (Asean) summit is the Quad leaders’ first since Trump’s January 2025 return to power, and comes after his Republican party took a drubbing in this month’s midterm elections.

While the Quad – broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence – has quietly progressed in deepening coordination, the short time allotted for Tuesday’s meeting meant it was unlikely to extend beyond pleasantries, Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution told AFP.
The timing, however, carried significance, he said, given the historic meeting Trump will attend with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in just two days.
“It’s a way of inoculating Trump against criticism of caving to authoritarians when he meets with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen,” Hass said.
This would be the first ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China.

Hayley Channer, economic security director at the Sydney-based United States Studies Centre, said Trump’s decision to include Asean on his travel agenda was noteworthy, as “South-eastt Asia has never been a high priority for the United States”.
Tariffs and chips
Japan’s foreign ministry said the Quad agenda would include discussions of the East and South China Sea – areas where multiple parties have overlapping claims with China.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

US President Donald Trump (back centre) takes part in a Quad leaders’ meeting with Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi (front, second left), India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the Solaire Resort on the sidelines of the 49th Asean Summit in Manila on November 17, 2026. — AFP pic
Trump will later attend a meeting with Asean heads of state before going to a gala dinner.
While Asean leaders have spent three days grappling with a raft of regional issues, the spectre of Trump’s ongoing tariff blitz has loomed large.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Monday slammed what he called a “countercurrent of unilateralism and protectionism” while touting Beijing’s own expanding trade with the bloc.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Canada’s Mark Carney sang a similar tune on trade, with both explicitly citing a need to wean themselves off dependence on the US market.
Trump’s arrival comes on the heels of an announced US rules shift on the transfer of advanced AI chips, a move that could potentially rankle Asean members.
Companies shipping high-end chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will now require a special licence, as the countries were said to represent a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion”.
Singapore responded by saying it was now exploring ways to facilitate “trusted access” for firms based in the city-state.
Pax Silica
Trump is set to meet with Philippine leader Ferdinand Marcos at the presidential palace on Wednesday before heading to China’s Shenzhen.
Channer, from the US Studies Centre, said the Manila visit was “likely because the US is trying to further its Pax Silica initiative, to build a complete mine-to-chip supply chain”.

Aimed at countering China’s dominance in semiconductors and rare earths, the initiative has been the focus of months of protests in the Philippines, as its flagship 1,620-hectare (about 4,000-acre) AI manufacturing hub north of Manila threatens to displace Indigenous families.

“We are gathered here today to call for the stop of Pax Silica and to save the lands of the Filipino people,” Mariposa, a 21-year-old drag queen, told AFP at Tuesday’s protest while wearing a long black cape emblazoned with the words “Pax Silica Sashay Away!”
US Ambassador Lee Lipton, a Trump appointee, said last week that a long-rumoured deal signing for the site would not take place during the president’s visit. — AFP
602ad92eb82a12fa: BRUSSELS: France and Belgium must bring down their public debt and deficit levels, EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis warned on Tuesday.
Under EU rules, the public deficit – the annual shortfall of revenue to spending – is meant to be no more than 3% of GDP, and debt must not be above 60% of GDP.
Both France and Belgium have deficits above 5% of GDP and debt of more than 110% of GDP and face mounting political turbulence.

Dombrovskis, however, appeared sanguine, telling reporters in Brussels, "We see sufficient demand for French sovereign and also Belgian sovereign debt, so we do not see any imminent financial stability issue."
But, he added, "clearly with this level of spreads it is important to make sure that deficit and debt are put on a downwards trajectory", referring to their increasing borrowing costs.

In France, the EU's second-biggest economy, prime minister Sebastien Lecornu is struggling to pass a deficit-cutting budget for 2027 in a parliament where President Emmanuel Macron's centrists no longer hold a majority.
International investors have expressed widespread concern over France's debt level, and this has pushed up the interest yields it pays to service debt, which is one of the highest in Europe.
The country will hold a two-round presidential election in April-May 2027, and there are concerns over how France would be able to cut debt after the vote.
France's debt level is expected to be 119.2% of GDP in 2026, the commission said, while its deficit this year will be 5.5% of GDP.
The EU expects French debt to keep rising to more than 123% of GDP in 2028, and Belgium's debt will reach more than 115% in the same year.

In Belgium, prime minister Bart De Wever is scrambling to get a new cost-cutting budget with his governing partners over the line. Failure to strike a deal could potentially bring down his government.
Belgium's debt level is expected to be 111.2% of GDP in 2026, according to the commission forecast, while its deficit is 5.2% of GDP this year.
The EU executive will next week make its recommendations on member states' budgets, including those in the sin bin over high deficit levels.

a17a1ebe1019c76e: BATU PAHAT, Nov 17 — Two women in Batu Pahat and Kuala Terengganu suffered combined losses of over RM1.18 million after being duped by phone scammers posing as police officers.
In Batu Pahat, a secondary school teacher suffered losses amounting to RM748,326.50 after falling victim to a phone scam involving a suspect posing as a Bukit Aman police officer.

Batu Pahat district police chief ACP Shahrulanuar Mushaddat Abdullah Sani said the 54-year-old woman received a call in late August from an unidentified individual claiming to be from a hospital in Rawang, Selangor.
He said during the phone conversation, the victim was informed that a third party had used her name to make an insurance claim before the call was transferred to the purported police officer.
“The suspect told the victim that he would help her lodge a police report online and also asked her to hand over her ATM card for an investigation by Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM).
“Out of fear, the victim followed the suspect’s instructions, including leaving her ATM card at a nasi lemak stall next to her house on September 3,” he said in a statement today.
Shahrulanuar said the victim checked her bank account last week and discovered several money transfers totalling RM673,326.50 to accounts belonging to unknown individuals.
The victim had also deposited RM75,000 into three different bank accounts on November 4, before recounting the incident to her elder sister on Sunday and realising that she had been scammed.
In a separate case, a 63-year-old retiree in Kuala Terengganu lost RM436,000 after falling victim to a phone scam with a similar modus operandi.

Kuala Terengganu district police chief ACP Azli Mohd Noor said the victim was contacted by a suspect posing as a police officer in early October, claiming that she was involved in money laundering activities and her bank account had been blacklisted by BNM for further investigation.

“The suspect instructed the victim to pawn her jewellery and deposit the money into a bank account. She was also told to leave her bank card beside a rubbish bin at a supermarket in Kuala Nerus. Fearing legal action, the victim complied with the instructions,” he said in a statement today.
Azli said the victim realised that her money was missing after obtaining a bank statement yesterday and saw withdrawals totalling RM436,036 between October 13 and November 4.
The victim lodged a police report at 1.26pm yesterday.
Both cases are being investigated under Section 420 of the Penal Code. — Bernama

da9f32eb9df82f74: SHAH ALAM, Nov 17 — The Selangor state government is formulating a stricter policy to improve enforcement and coordination at commercial chicken slaughterhouses, including a proposal requiring licensed premises to employ at least one certified halal slaughterer.

He said 60 slaughterhouses in Selangor were licensed by local authorities (PBT), while another 149 had certified halal slaughterers but no PBT licences.

“At present, the management is somewhat fragmented, as licensing matters fall under the PBT, while halal slaughtering matters are under the Selangor Islamic Religious Department (JAIS),” he told a press conference at the Selangor State Legislative Assembly (DUN) building here today.

Mohammad Fahmi said inspections by local authorities had identified five slaughterhouses in Subang Jaya and Kuala Langat that had neither operating licences nor certified halal slaughterers. Enforcement action, including seizures, had been taken against the premises.

cad1369bb5e3c359: BRUSSELS: Temu could face a second hefty EU fine after Brussels accused the Chinese-owned online retailer on Tuesday of failing to protect consumers from the sale of unsafe items.
The EU already ordered a €200 million (US$220 million) fine on Temu in May for allowing the sale of illegal products, including dangerous baby toys and defective chargers.

Now the European Commission said Temu was breaking more rules under the Digital Services Act (DSA) by failing "to put in place reasonable, proportionate and effective measures to mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered".
Temu said it "respectfully" disagreed with the commission's preliminary view.
The retailer is popular in the EU, with more than 120 million users after entering the bloc's market in 2023.
Under the DSA, fines can go as high as 6% of a company's total worldwide annual turnover.

Tuesday's findings are about the measures Temu is taking to protect EU users, a senior European official said, whereas the fine in May focused on the failure to conduct a proper risk assessment to understand what dangers the platform poses.
'Making the online world safer'
The EU said Temu did not have effective controls in place to check whether products complied with the bloc's safety requirements.
High-risk categories include toys, electronics and cosmetics.

Brussels also said Temu's sanction system was not a strong enough deterrent, with traders able to commit several serious infringements – such as selling products that fail safety checks – before Temu suspended any of their stores.

EU regulators found Temu's moderation system did not prevent unsafe and illegal products from being offered to consumers and appeared to focus more on complying with the company's rules than a product's safety.
"Shopping online should not mean risking the purchase of illegal and unsafe products," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
"The preliminary findings against Temu mark another step towards making the online world safer," she added.
Small package levies
The DSA law is part of the EU's wide-ranging legal toolbox for oversight of the world's biggest online retailers, social media platforms and search engines.
Temu now has the right to examine the EU's documents and reply in writing.
The company said it "invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks".
"We will review and respond to the preliminary findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the commission," it said.
The Temu investigation that began in 2024 is one of many under the DSA, including probes into China's AliExpress and the Chinese-founded Shein.
The EU in July imposed a fine of €550 million on AliExpress over the sale of illegal goods on its platform.
Consumers are buying more items from outside the EU, often because of the cheaper prices, but Brussels is cracking down on small parcel imports.
Last year, nearly six billion small packages entered the bloc, mostly from China, up from around 4.6 billion in 2024.
The EU this month set a €2 handling fee on packages from outside the bloc, coming just months after imposing a three-euro levy on low-cost parcels.

8d09a058f8d4043b: As many as 99 percent of Britain's civil servants rely on Microsoft to communicate, a government minister has admitted, days after Redmond demonstrated the perils of putting quite so many eggs in one basket.

Ian Murray, minister for creative industries, media and online safety, laid bare the extent of Whitehall's Microsoft habit in the House of Commons on Monday, where MPs were also told that the public sector shelled out £1.9 billion on Microsoft licenses in 2024-25 alone.
"We know that 98% to 99% of civil servants use Microsoft as their platform for communications, which is incredibly high," Murray told MPs.

The admission followed last week's 18-hour Microsoft 365 outage, which left businesses unable to carry out transactions, public sector workers struggling to do their jobs, and even MPs unable to access their usual means of communication.

Rebecca Paul, shadow technology secretary, said at least 47 NHS trusts experienced problems, with some services having to fall back on pen and paper. The Conservative MP, who cited the £1.9 billion licensing bill, pressed Murray on whether the government would seek contractual remedies from Microsoft.

Murray said the government was unaware of any delays to NHS treatment or instances in which patients had been put at risk. Emergency departments remained open, and 999 services continued to operate. Only two NHS trusts activated incident response units, the minister said.

The outage, which affected 74 countries, has since been blamed on a software update Microsoft rolled out in July. A surge in Teams traffic hit infrastructure already short of server capacity, exposing the months-old bug. More than 80 percent of the servers in the affected gateway stopped responding, leaving Redmond's engineers scrambling to fix their previous fix.
Much of Monday's discussion centered on how the UK had allowed itself to become so dependent on a handful of American technology companies in the first place.

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of Parliament's Science and Technology Committee, pointed out that the government had been unable to tell her committee how much it spends on IT and which suppliers it uses. She also challenged ministers over their reluctance to embrace open source software, something both France and Germany have pursued to loosen Big Tech's grip on their public sectors.

“Germany has 500,000 civil servants using open source products and services, but the government told my Committee that though open source could address vendor lock-in, they would not include open source targets because of a lack of what was called ‘commercial accountability’,” she said.
Paul, meanwhile, reminded Murray that just last month the government had rejected the committee's recommendation to introduce supplier diversification targets.

Murray conceded that the government's extensive dealings with Microsoft probably result in "vendor lock-in," but defended the arrangement, saying it gives Whitehall access to the latest technology at scale.
The admission comes less than a week after research from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) revealed just how little of the British public sector's IT budget ends up in British hands.

Of the £19.2 billion spent with the public sector's 150 biggest technology suppliers in 2024-25, just 15 percent went to businesses headquartered and owned in the UK, with a predominantly British workforce and which weren't reselling overseas technology. American companies took home almost twice as much as suppliers from all other foreign countries combined.

Murray said the government intends to use its considerable purchasing power to give British businesses a leg up. Its national cloud infrastructure program will see departments procure cloud services collectively rather than individually, with the intention of giving more suppliers a crack at lucrative government contracts.

Whitehall has also set up a technology risk group and a central IT operations function to scrutinize outages and work out what needs fixing across the public sector. Ministers intend to press Microsoft on how it plans to prevent a repeat of last week's cock-up and whether it can get services back online more quickly next time.

The government, however, offered no timetable for weaning civil servants off Microsoft's software, nor did Murray commit to targets for adopting open-source alternatives. Redmond's days as Whitehall's IT supplier of choice hardly look numbered. ®

63b3946a17a6e71f: SYDNEY, Nov 17 — A dead Australian racehorse has been found in an industrial rubbish bin on the outskirts of Sydney two weeks after running in the prestigious Melbourne Cup.

“Like everyone who has seen the footage I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are’s remains,” Baker said in a statement on social media.

“After his death So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried,” the company said.
“What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone else who cared for him.
Racing NSW said So You Are was awaiting burial when video of the abandoned horse was recorded, and the footage was subsequently shared online.
“The way in which So You Are’s body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable.
“So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect,” the regulating body in New South Wales state said in a statement, according to ABC.

Earlier, Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) deputy public prosecutor Nurdeenie Abdul Rashid proposed bail of RM50,000 for each accused, with the additional condition that their passports be surrendered to the court.

However, their lawyer Mohammed Fudhail Ahmad Zulaini sought a reduction on the grounds that his clients are supporting five children aged between six and 18, and had cooperated well with the authorities throughout the investigation.

4babfe9bec385cb4: SAN FRANCISCO: US chip titan Nvidia said Tuesday it had created an oversight committee for national security and export control in the wake of a spy scandal that forced chief Jensen Huang to quit.

3206a7ab101184bb: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 17 — Students who assist lecturers in developing innovations, including prototypes with commercial potential, should receive royalties in recognition of their contributions and efforts.

Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said the contributions of students directly involved in the research and development of a product should be recognised alongside those of the lecturers leading the innovation.
“Do not forget that the people helping the lecturers are students who also contribute to the work.

“Students must receive royalties. It should not be just the lecturers who benefit. Students must also receive their share because they have worked equally hard,” he said when officiating the Putrajaya Festival of Ideas 2026 here today.
Ahmad Zahid said universities should also establish clear pathways for promising ideas, from prototype development and patent applications to industry adoption or commercialisation.

He said universities and the Higher Education Ministry should provide networks, funding and implementation partners to ensure researchers were not left to pursue their work on their own after making a discovery.
He said lecturers and researchers should also receive continued support following their discoveries, including greater opportunities for career development and promotion.

Ahmad Zahid said Malaysia must also dare to set ambitious goals to produce discoveries capable of changing the world while ensuring that the benefits of technological and innovation advancements were enjoyed by the people.

He said the success of research and innovation should not be measured solely by academic achievements, but also by the tangible benefits they brought to society, including farmers seeking to increase agricultural yields, young people looking for quality jobs and families striving for a better life.

“That is where the greatness of technology finds its human meaning. If every major transformation in civilisation begins with the power of human thought, let the ideas emerging from the Putrajaya Festival of Ideas be the starting point for Malaysia’s next great leap,” he said.
He also stressed that universities should be open spaces for testing ideas and debating different perspectives, while nurturing students who are willing to think critically.
Students, he said, should not rely solely on memorisation or accept views without question, but must have the courage to ask questions, construct arguments and offer solutions. — Bernama

2ec83782fbfee98b: Lawmakers and campaign groups have slammed the UK government's decision to extend Palantir's controversial NHS contract by two years.

Health minister James Frith told MPs on Monday that the current contract would continue until March 2029 as the government procures a new version of the Federated Data Platform (FDP). The existing Palantir-led deal, awarded in 2023, has a maximum value of £330 million and includes other suppliers.

Frith said the new procurement would focus on interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards in a "new FDP iteration" which would "welcome international and UK capability alike – whether that is UK small and medium-sized enterprises that want a crack at NHS contracts, sovereign AI-backed capability in the UK or any international provider worth merit."

Palantir's cornerstone NHS contract win attracted criticism for lack of transparency. The US supplier had already won £60 million in NHS contracts without competition during and following the pandemic. Use cases from this period were carried over to the FDP. Critics have also challenged the evidence used to promote the FDP's claimed benefits.

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, said she was "extremely disappointed" by the decision. She challenged the government's reliance on continuity of care to justify keeping the contract, given its existing transition provisions. She said Palantir made it clear it would use the next two years to "embed itself even more deeply in our public services."

"If a break clause cannot be exercised because of continuity of care, it is not a break clause; it is a lock-in. The Minister assured me that there were already contractual requirements that smooth continuity of care should continue. Were those assurances made in error?" she asked Frith.
Frith confirmed that the contracts included exit and transition provisions and that migration was "possible in principle."

"However, given the requirement for a new iteration, given performance and the benefits already in play, and given the opportunity to add new capability, including maternity services, to a next generation of FDP, an 18 to 24-month period for commission and procurement is a reasonable assessment," he said.

Technology and government priorities had moved on since the original FDP procurement in 2023, he told MPs. "We will begin a new procurement process along different lines from the current contract," he said.
The formal process is set to start during the second half of next year and take around 18 months.

"Interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards can and must be baked into the next generation of FDP. We will also start work, alongside the new procurement, with different providers on developing new capabilities and expertise starting with systems used in maternity care. Innovative providers will be invited to help address the data and digital fragmentation in this important area of care, and test how health priorities can create routes to build UK AI capability," Frith said.
Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, now Palantir's UK senior vice president, welcomed the extension.

"This is good news for patients and for the NHS. And it is the right decision to press forward with a programme that, in the words of Ministers, 'is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target' since it launched in 2024," he said.

"We will now redouble our efforts over the next two years to continue and accelerate that support. As a result of the announcement, we will also deepen our investment in the UK. The FDP is the right vehicle to deliver the change needed in the NHS, and over the next two years Palantir will do everything in its power to drive that change as far as possible, as fast as possible."
Nonprofit tech transparency group Foxglove has challenged NHS contracts awarded to Palantir without competition since the pandemic, when the company initially offered its services for £1.

Responding to the extension, Foxglove co-executive director Rosa Curling said: "Palantir and its chief lobbyist Lord Tom Watson clearly think the contract extension is in the bag and appear to be already planning to turn that into another extension in two years, or a new procurement that heavily favors Palantir as we saw in 2023.

"The government must provide urgent clarity on whether they plan to help Watson embed Palantir in the NHS for the long term – or will kick this Trump-backing spy tech company out of the health service once and for all." ®

9707f7db38eaca92: BERLIN: Shares in Deutsche Bank plunged on Tuesday after international media outlets published reports based on millions of leaked emails and other documents that shine a light on questionable past business practices at the German banking giant.
The leaks deal with the bank's business over the past 20 years, including ties to Russian oligarchs, the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and Donald Trump before he became US president.

The data, shared by unidentified whistleblowers, raised questions about internal controls at Germany's largest bank and reignited questions regarding chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution.

The investigation, dubbed "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.
Deutsche Bank shares fell by nearly 6% shortly after the opening of the Frankfurt Stock Exchange.
According to the reports, the bank at times prioritised commercial interests over compliance with international sanctions, anti-money laundering regulations and even its own internal procedures.
The data originated from two whistleblowers and was channelled through South African and Indian journalists to more than 50 media outlets worldwide.

The documents reportedly detail, among other things, how Deutsche Bank courted oligarchs and sought to expand its Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.
Documents cited by the media outlets indicate that Sewing was among the participants in the working group that developed the Russia strategy.
The reports also note that the bank's announced withdrawal from the Russian market after the Ukraine invasion remains incomplete.
As of last year, Deutsche Bank still employed 162 people in the country, and its local subsidiary generated a pre-tax profit of €61 million (US$67 million).
The data also contain new details regarding the bank's long-standing business relationship with Epstein as well as its dealings with Trump.
Furthermore, the documents indicate that the bank set up controversial tax-optimisation schemes for wealthy clients and suggest that criminal networks were able to funnel money through the bank.

The documents also offer insights into arms deals involving problematic states, the bank's support for clients in environmentally damaging industries, and the holding of donation accounts for Germany's far-right AfD political party despite internal opposition.
Deutsche Bank does not dispute that the records are genuine, though it refers to them as "purported internal documents" and noted that some of the incidents cited date back more than two decades.
The bank said that it reviewed these matters with regulatory authorities at the time and that it had invested seven billion euros between 2019 and 2025 to strengthen its control systems.
It is now "a different bank", it said, pointing to record profits in 2025 and progress made in terms of compliance.

08ef85fa531ac909: PostgreSQL developers have patched 52 security vulnerabilities and more than 140 bugs in updates spanning versions 14 to 18, alongside a second release candidate for version 19.
The batch includes PostgreSQL 14.25, the final release for the now-unsupported version 14. Users are advised to move to a newer major version.
Some fixes also require follow-up work, including rebuilding affected indexes or taking a fresh full backup. Administrators should check the release's post-update instructions.
Alastair Turner, community technologist at open source consultancy Percona, said the high-severity code execution flaws should be taken seriously, although exploiting them requires database access.

"This isn't something just a brute-force scan of the right port is going to find," he said. "They can make compromises through SQL injection or credential theft a lot worse, but don't create the opportunity for remote, anonymous code execution."
Among the fixes is CVE-2026-6460, a type confusion flaw that could let a database user with permission to create objects execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS severity score of 8.8 out of 10.
Turner attributed the growing number of security discoveries partly to AI-assisted scanning and partly to increased scrutiny as PostgreSQL gains ground in enterprise computing.

"It is a record number of CVEs fixed in a quarterly release, and I don't think we've seen the end of that trend. Looking down the list of where these CVEs came from, we see Anthropic and OpenAI open source scanners, so it is clear AI or brute force is playing a role," he said.
Turner said the fixes spanned multiple parts of the software. There "isn't one piece of code that was broken" but rather "a wide base that got patched."
"It's also worth noting that this is the third quarterly release in a row which sets a new record for the number of CVEs patched," he added.

PostgreSQL 14 users now face a major-version upgrade or running without further security and bug fixes. Their destination may depend on internal upgrade policies. Organizations that require the previous major release, known as N-1, would currently target PostgreSQL 17, Turner noted. Version 18 remains the latest generally available release until 19 arrives.

PostgreSQL 19 is scheduled for general availability on Thursday, November 19, barring further problems. It is set to include a new REPACK command, whose CONCURRENTLY option allows reads and writes to continue while disk space is reclaimed. VACUUM FULL requires an exclusive table lock, blocking reads and writes while it runs. ®

7229b624ba3968fe: BENGALURU: Some of the world's most visited websites, including those belonging to Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and IKEA, were subverted in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, a security researcher said on Monday.
Malicious JavaScript was aimed at visitors to the websites of 178 organizations across various sectors through Optimizely, a website optimization platform, according to researcher Scott Helme.

The scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency payment addresses with the attacker's wallet, skim card numbers as users entered credit card details, steal cookies and screenshots, and plant exploit code on iOS devices.
Cybersecurity firm HudsonRock also said it had found evidence that the sites had served malicious code to their visitors.
Reuters could not immediately ascertain whether the code was successfully used in each case, or the extent of any resulting hacks.
Salesforce said it was investigating unauthorized Optimizely script changes, and had disabled them as a precaution.
Equifax also looked into the issue. It stopped using Optimizely and found no evidence that its systems were compromised.
IKEA said it was seeking to determine if there was any potential impact on its digital services and customers.
Optimizely, Apple, Zoom, HSBC, and CNN did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
bbe09e724f0f57a4: WASHINGTON, Nov 17 — AI chip giant Nvidia reports its first earnings on Tuesday since a spy scandal forced co-founder Jensen Huang to quit and the United States to tighten export curbs on chips.
Investors will closely scrutinize the results for indications the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.

Huang, perhaps the tech industry’s most recognised booster of artificial intelligence, stepped down on Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The scandal has battered shares of Nvidia – until recently the world’s most valuable publicly traded company – which is at the centre of an AI buildout that has helped propel markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the globe.

Washington announced new restrictions on Monday on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing just before the high-profile APEC summit where US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are set for talks.
Beijing’s foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said “China will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.

The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over Trump and Xi’s talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting, which starts Wednesday in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

The rules also require licenses to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US commerce department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.

The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.
While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.

His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.

The scandal has exposed a rift within the Trump administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accusing the commerce department of ignoring reports that Megaspeed was shifting Nvidia technology to China.
The US government confirmed on Monday it was investigating Megaspeed, with the commerce department launching a probe in 2024 for potential export control violations.
‘Business-as-usual’ unlikely
Tuesday’s third quarter results, which are scheduled for 5:00 pm ET (2200 GMT), will be the first presented under Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO.
“If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn’t be well received,” said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer.
Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.
Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia’s guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore.

That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy – with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Thursday.
Tech firms dragged Asian stock markets down again Tuesday as the fallout from the Nvidia crisis rattles trading floors, with the new US moves on chip controls adding to uncertainty.
On Tuesday, Singapore said it was engaging with affected companies and talking to US authorities to ascertain the scope and implementation of the new measures.
The city-state is also “exploring how to facilitate trusted access (to AI chips) for Singapore companies”, a government statement said.
Indonesia said it was reviewing the measure “and seeking industry input on its potential impact on operations and investment, including in the data centre sector”. — AFP
08ce2b4128756871: CYBERJAYA: The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) has appointed TM Technology Services Sdn Bhd (TM) as the universal service provider for designing, implementing, and operating the Madani Submarine Cable Connection System (Salam) worth RM2.7 billion.
MCMC said in a statement that the project would be funded through the Universal Service Provision (USP) Fund.
The Salam system will enhance communication connection capacity between Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak.

"It simultaneously supports the provision of more reliable digital services to the community, businesses and government. In addition, it will also provide an alternative route for data traffic, thereby reducing the risk of service disruption in the event the existing undersea cables experience interference or damage," said MCMC.
With a length of approximately 5,500km, the system will be implemented by TM based on Alcatel Submarine Networks's (ASN) submarine cable technology and will meet increasing demand.
The capacity utilisation of the existing submarine cable network, which has been in operation since 2017, has now reached about 85%.

MCMC said the Salam system would include 10 new submarine cable landing stations, namely Cherating and Sedili in Peninsular Malaysia; Kuching, Sibu (Matu) and Bintulu (Samalaju) in Sarawak; as well as Kota Kinabalu, Kudat, Pulau Banggi, Sandakan and Tawau in Sabah.

The additional capacity will support the expansion of broadband and 5G networks, cloud services, artificial intelligence, and data centres, thereby providing a stronger foundation to expand digital capacity, particularly in Sabah and Sarawak.
"Four pairs of optical fibre will be dedicated to meet the strategic needs of the nation, including sovereign cloud infrastructure, government digital services and cybersecurity.
"Salam reflects MCMC's commitment to strengthening Malaysia's digital infrastructure so that more communities and businesses can enjoy the benefits of the digital economy," said MCMC.

4111a81bc2e14429: The court ruled that soldiers who committed criminal offenses should be tried by civilian courts
Originally published on Global Voices
Constitutional Court of Indonesia in Jakarta. Photo by Christophe95. Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Indonesia’s Constitutional Court ruled that the 1997 Military Justice Law would be invalid unless amended within two years. The decision was hailed by human rights groups because it means soldiers who commit crimes can be tried in civilian courts.

Article 9 of the Military Justice Law requires active-duty personnel of the Indonesian National Armed Forces to be held accountable exclusively under the military justice system, even when they commit ordinary criminal offenses and human rights violations.
The law was a legacy of the New Order era when the country was under the strongman rule of Suharto, who relied on the military establishment to hold power from 1966 until his resignation in 1998.

The October 15 court ruling was celebrated by human rights groups that have long advocated for the overhaul of the law. They have documented how military courts have failed to investigate and prosecute grave abuses committed by soldiers. They have also expressed concern that military judges are active-duty soldiers, and that judicial investigations and prosecutions often take place within the military chain of command and behind closed doors, with no public oversight.

One of the petitioners asking officials to revoke the law was Eva Meliani Pasaribu, the daughter of Tribrata TV journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu, who was killed in June 2024 after reporting about a gambling operation allegedly involving a high-level military official. The military conducted a closed-door investigation and dismissed the allegation for lack of evidence.
Ibnu Syamsu Hidayat, the legal counsel for the petition, addressed the court during the hearing and explained how the law erodes civilian supremacy within a democratic system of governance.

“The dominance of military court jurisdiction over the general judiciary is considered inconsistent with the principles of a constitutional democracy, which mandates that civilian authority must take precedence over military power.”
Hidayat added that the law’s broad provisions have been interpreted to include other criminal offenses committed by soldiers.

“It allows them not only to try military personnel or those equated with them for military crimes and disciplinary violations, but also to adjudicate other criminal cases such as corruption, traffic offenses, domestic violence, narcotics, psychotropics, and child protection cases.”

During the hearing, numerous high-level military officers spoke up in defense of the law. The director general of Defense Forces at the Ministry of Defense, Marshal H. Haris Haryanto, argued that the actions of soldiers, including criminal violations, “can also affect the solidarity and readiness of the military institution.” He added, “Military courts are designed to understand these characteristics so they can deliver decisions that satisfy a sense of justice while also taking into account the interests of national defense.”

The commander of the National Armed Forces, General Agus Subiyanto, said the petition questioning the effectiveness, independence, and accountability of the military justice system “is not based on a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics of military law.”

He emphasized that military judges have the independence of judicial power guaranteed by the constitution and are under the technical judicial supervision of the Supreme Court, adding, “In a military organization, discipline is the primary foundation of national strength. Therefore, the commander’s authority to ensure due process for his subordinates is an inherent legal obligation to maintain operational readiness and the institution’s honor.”

Legal experts who participated in the hearing disagreed, arguing that the law needs reform in order to comply with current human rights standards. Al Araf told the court that the law was drafted under the framework of an “authoritarian political regime” that ignored the principles of rule of law.

“During the New Order era, the legal products enacted in the form of statutes tended to be repressive and merely served as instruments of control for those in power,” he said. “The state enacted laws not within the framework of the rule of law, but solely to fulfill the needs of the rule by law.”
Zainal Arifin Mochtar, another legal expert at the hearing, said the law has to be updated to conform with democratic principles.

“Many issues have emerged, ranging from dual jurisdictions, a lack of synchronization with the spirit of reform, the absence of detailed regulations regarding connectivity, to the issue of independence and accountability of military justice, which is often discussed as a form of legal exceptionalism,” he said.

The move has been widely celebrated by human rights defenders. The Indonesian human rights group KontraS welcomed the court decision, noting that one of its employees has been subjected to an acid attack perpetrated by a group of soldiers. Under the new ruling, soldiers could be tried in public courts in such cases.

“This ruling closes a legal loophole that has long been perceived as protecting individual soldiers from accountable law enforcement, while also marking a new chapter in upholding the rule of law and fulfilling the mandate of security sector reform in Indonesia,” read their statement.
The reform is the result of decades of work and activism, as explained by Human Rights Watch (HRW).

“Justice for civilian victims of military abuses shouldn’t be blocked by an unfair military court system,” read their statement. “Amending the law on military justice will support efforts begun decades ago to ensure the Indonesian military is a professional, credible institution whose soldiers are held accountable when they commit serious abuses.”
Free Press Unlimited said the court ruling is a victory against impunity.

“The Constitutional Court’s eagerly awaited ruling is a true victory for justice and a critical step for Indonesia in its fight against impunity,” read their statement on the ruling. “We urge lawmakers to act promptly and adhere to this landmark ruling as soon as possible. Only then can Indonesia finally turn a corner and ensure that cases involving military personnel will be dealt with by civilian courts, as it should be.”

Both Indonesian and international civil society groups are urging lawmakers to start the reform process by consulting the public and various stakeholders. Activists argue that public vigilance has to be sustained, especially since Indonesia’s current president, Prabowo Subianto, is a former general dismissed from the military for committing human rights violations. Since coming to power in 2024, he has expanded the military’s role in civilian governance.
Written by Mong Palatino

677a251ae49efcfd: WASHINGTON, Nov 17 — The United States announced tougher export control measures on AI chips Monday, after a scandal ensnaring Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang exposed a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.
The news came the day before Californian chip titan Nvidia reports its first earnings since Huang’s departure as CEO, with investors questioning if the artificial intelligence boom can hold strong.

Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

The rules also requires licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US commerce department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.

These changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.

While this loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Nvidia co-founder Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.

The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in violation of export controls.
Jensen Huang, 63, stepped down last week after at least two extramarital affairs were revealed in media reports.
Facing criticism, the US Commerce Department said Monday it would close a loophole that had drawn concern from US authorities.

The move “is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement.
It weighed on Nvidia’s shares, which shed four per cent on Monday, extending a slide since the scandal erupted.
‘Business-as-usual’ unlikely
Nvidia stock has lost more than a quarter of its value over the past month, as doubts grow about the health of the AI investment boom.
Tuesday’s results will be the first presented under chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO.
“If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn’t be well received,” said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer, describing the company as in turmoil.
Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.
Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia’s guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore.

That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy – with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Thursday.
Tech firms dragged Asian stock markets down again Tuesday as the fallout from the Nvidia crisis rattles trading floors, with the new US moves on chip controls adding to uncertainty.
‘Trusted access’
On Tuesday Singapore said it was engaging with affected companies and talking to US authorities to ascertain the scope and implementation of the new measures.
The city-state is also “exploring how to facilitate trusted access (to AI chips) for Singapore companies”, a government statement said.
Indonesia said it was reviewing the measure “and seeking industry input on its potential impact on operations and investment, including in the data centre sector”.
The scandal has exposed a rift within the Trump administration.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for an investigation into Jensen Huang’s dealings with Megaspeed, and accuses the Commerce Department of ignoring widespread reports that Megaspeed was shifting Nvidia technology to China.
Tech tycoon Elon Musk and other major AI investors are meanwhile gathering signatures for an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.
“The most important time to help someone is when they’re down,” investor Bill Ackman said at a Semafor tech conference.
Before leaving for summits in Asia, President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, waving off the security concerns.
But given the legal cloud over him, most Wall Street analysts doubt that the AI rock star can return anytime soon.
Kress, a non-engineer, is not expected to stay in the role permanently, leaving Nvidia facing a high-stakes search for a successor. — AFP
